lines: A doctor drank a broth full of living stomach bacteria.
He was trying to make himself sick.
For decades, doctors blamed stomach ulcers on stress, spicy food and too much acid.
But in Perth, Australia, Barry Marshall and Robin Warren suspected a spiral-shaped bacterium.
Many doctors ridiculed the idea.
No bacteria could live in stomach acid, they said.
Reviewers ranked the pair's paper among the worst they got that year.
Marshall tried to infect piglets. It failed.
So in 1984, he made himself the test.
You see, it's like tasting milk to check if it's gone sour.
Sometimes the only proof is your own stomach.
First, doctors checked his healthy stomach with a camera.
Then Marshall drank the broth.
He expected an ulcer, years later.
In just three days, he felt sick.
His wife noticed his terrible breath.
Then the vomiting started.
On day eight, the camera went back in.
His stomach was badly inflamed, and the bacteria had moved in.
Marshall took antibiotics and recovered.
In 2005, the idea doctors had ridiculed won Marshall and Warren the Nobel Prize.

claims.claim: Marshall drank a broth containing cultured H. pylori, expecting to develop an ulcer years later.
Medical doctrine held that ulcers were caused primarily by stress, spicy foods and too much acid.
Marshall and Robin Warren at Royal Perth Hospital studied spiral bacteria in association with gastritis and proposed a bacterial cause of peptic ulcers.
The theory was ridiculed by doctors who did not believe bacteria could live in the acidic stomach; reviewers rated their paper in the bottom 10%.
After failed attempts to infect piglets in 1984, Marshall had a baseline endoscopy, then drank the broth.
In three days he had nausea and bad breath, noticed by his wife; on days 5-8 he vomited.
On day eight an endoscopy showed massive inflammation and H. pylori had colonised his stomach; he then took antibiotics.
In 2005 Marshall and Robin Warren were awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
